To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the ERS/ERD of the 4-6, 6-8, 8-10, and 10-12 Hz frequency bands is a reliable measure of the cortical activity changes during a memory task in healthy adults.
the ERD/ERS of the alpha band in the left and right parietal areas was correlated between the first and the second session.

the event-related desynchronisation (ERD) of the alpha and beta frequency bands (8-13 Hz), but not of the theta (4-8 Hz) and gamma (25-40 Hz) bands, was significantly reduced in the right hemisphere of the brain during a memory task, and that the ERD in the alpha band was significantly correlated with the memory task performance.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new type of brain-computer interface (BCI), which is based on a new type of EEG-based BCI paradigm, called the “imagined movement BCI” (iMBCI) paradigm.
the development of a new type of brain-computer interface (BCI), based on the event-related desynchronisation/synchronisation (ERD/ERS) phenomenon.
the study of brain activity in the alpha and beta frequency bands during the performance of memory tasks.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the event-related desynchronisation (ERD) and event-related synchronization (ERS) of the alpha band are not a reliable measure of the attentional processes in the human brain.
the ERD/ERS of the 4-6, 6-8, 8-10 and 10-12 Hz frequency bands is a reliable measure of the brain activity during the memory task, with a high level of consistency between sessions.

the event-related desynchronisation (ERD) is a robust and reliable method to measure cortical activity during cognitive tasks, and that the test-retest reliability of the 4-8 Hz frequency band in the frontal and temporal areas is higher than that in the occipital and parietal areas.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the EEG signal is a very rich source of information, which is not only useful for the detection of epileptic seizures, but also for the analysis and understanding of cognitive processes.
the 4–8 and 8–12 Hz bands are more consistent than the 10–12 and 4–6 Hz bands, and the latter two bands are more consistent in the frontal than in the parietal areas.
the event-related desynchronisation (ERD) and event-related synchronisation (ERS) are not consistent across subjects, and the ERD/ERS is not consistent in the frequency band.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the event-related desynchronisation (ERD) is a reliable and robust measure that can be used to study cognitive processes, such as working memory.

the 4–8 Hz frequency band, which is known to contain the mu rhythm and the alpha rhythm, is the most sensitive frequency band for the assessment of the cognitive state of the human brain, and that the alpha and beta frequency bands are less suitable for that purpose.

we can now use a single electrode to detect the event-related desynchronisation (ERD) and synchronisation (ERS) of the EEG signal in the 4-6, 6-8, 8-10 and 10-12 Hz bands, which is the first step towards a wearable device to detect cognitive states.
